opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Natalie, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how changes at work affect people's lives. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happy to, though it's strange being the one answering for once. I'm a reporter at the regional paper. Council meetings, courts, the local stuff nobody else covers anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a better search tool is fine, but it doesn't sit through a three-hour council meeting. Local news needs reporters, not summaries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even in this version, the paper keeps shrinking. AI didn't halve our newsroom twice; falling ad money did. So 'no major impact' still means a slow decline for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it to transcribe interviews and search old council minutes, so I can spend more time out in town. And I'd keep pitching to bigger papers on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The usual, really.

S0.say: A search tool doesn't sit through a three-hour council meeting. Local news needs reporters, not summaries.
S0.think: Even here the paper keeps shrinking. Falling ad money halved our newsroom twice, not AI.
S0.do: Uses AI to transcribe interviews and search council minutes so she's out in town more, and keeps pitching to bigger papers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if no one hires young reporters, in ten years there's no one left to hold the powerful to account in towns like mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, slow means more AI-written filler in the paper, written from press releases, and fewer of us doing real reporting. I'm good at my job. I'm not sure the owners care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the stories a machine can't, the ones where you have to knock on doors. And I'd start looking into how non-profit local news sites are funded, in case I need a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see where it ends.

S1.say: If nobody hires young reporters, in ten years there'll be no one holding the powerful to account in towns like mine.
S1.think: Slow still means more AI filler from press releases and fewer real reporters. I'm good, but I'm not sure the owners care.
S1.do: Focuses on door-knocking stories a machine can't do, and researches how non-profit local news sites get funded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write about it. Media owners will use this to replace reporters with machines that rewrite press releases, and local democracy will pay for it. News should be treated as a public good and funded like one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my paper would cut again and use AI to fill the pages. There's one paper in this town. If I'm cut, I'm commuting two hours or leaving journalism.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union push for limits on AI in the newsroom, start a newsletter on local politics on the side, and talk to my partner about what we'd cut if I lost my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, edging toward something worse. I'd be awake at night doing the maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're good at your job. Wouldn't that keep you safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It kept me safe the last two rounds. But every round, being good counts for a bit less and being cheap counts for more.

S2.say: Media owners will replace reporters with machines rewriting press releases, and local democracy will pay. News should be funded as a public good.
S2.think: My paper would cut again and fill pages with AI. It's the only paper in town, so I'd be commuting two hours or leaving journalism.
S2.do: Joins the union push for limits on newsroom AI, starts a side newsletter on local politics and plans cuts with her partner.
S2.feel: Anxious, edging toward worse, doing sums at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a crisis for democracy, not just jobs. When nobody independent is watching the council, the rich and connected write the story. Tax the gains and fund public-interest news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the paper closes in this one, or becomes a website run by one editor and a machine. I'd be out, in a town with no other jobs like mine, with almost no savings and a kid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time on the newsletter and try to get the town to pay for it by subscription, apply to news charities for funding, and look at teaching or council comms jobs nearby, even though that's the side I used to report on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. And angry, which helps a little.

S3.say: This is a crisis for democracy, not just jobs. Tax the gains and fund public-interest news.
S3.think: The paper closes or becomes one editor and a machine. I'd be out, with almost no savings, a kid and no similar jobs in town.
S3.do: Goes full-time on her newsletter, seeks reader subscriptions and charity funding, and applies for teaching or council comms jobs nearby.
S3.feel: Alarmed and angry. The anger helps a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say now even the people who said 'learn a trade' can see it. We need to share the gains, all of us, together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots don't change my job, it was already gone. What they change is that my partner and I have no fallback at all. And the stories I'd want to cover would be huge, with no one paid to cover them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd lean even harder on the newsletter, because people would want to understand what's happening to their town. If it pays nothing, I'd still do it in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed. A grim sense of purpose, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep reporting even unpaid. Is that realistic with a child?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not for long. But I'd try. It's who I am. I'd find a day job and write at night until I couldn't.

S4.say: Even the people who said 'learn a trade' can see it now. We need to share the gains, together.
S4.think: My job was already gone. Now my partner and I have no fallback, and the biggest story of our lives would have no one paid to cover it.
S4.do: Leans harder on the newsletter, unpaid if needed, while finding a day job and writing at night.
S4.feel: Alarmed, with a grim sense of purpose.
